We aggregate the 38 attack flows into one graph, then split it into attack profiles by objective, such as stealing data.
We execute each attack profile in MTDSim, an existing MTD simulator , as the APT attacker model.
MTDSim's original scripted attacker, the baseline attacker, follows a fixed procedure of six attack actions, such as scanning a host's ports and exploiting its vulnerabilities.
We run both first with no MTD, then under each of MTDSim's seven MTD mechanisms at six deployment intervals, how often MTD changes the network.
If the same MTD mechanism is most effective against both attackers, an evaluation against the baseline attacker alone identifies it.
If they differ, the most effective MTD mechanism depends on the attacker model.

We find that, in MTDSim, the most effective MTD mechanism depends on the attacker model, so an evaluation against a single attacker model is not enough to show how MTD performs against other attackers.
It answers 1 and 1 by scoring the APT attacker model on the eight properties, and 1 by finding which MTD mechanisms are most effective against each attacker, and proposing why.
The APT attacker model is executed inside MTDSim, the MTD simulator this dissertation inherits, and compared with the simulator's baseline attacker.
What to move is a configurable attribute, such as an IP address, the network topology, an operating system or a piece of software.
How to move is one of three operations, the shuffle--diversity--redundancy (SDR) taxonomy .
Section 1 describes the network's hosts, services and vulnerabilities, Section 1 the MTD mechanisms and deployment strategies, and Section 1 the baseline attacker.
The first level is the exposed endpoints, the hosts reachable from outside the network.

Each vulnerability has an attack complexity from the Common Vulnerability Scoring System (CVSS), which sets the probability that an exploit succeeds, and an impact, the damage a successful exploit does .
The random, alternative and single deployment strategies follow a schedule, so they are proactive .

At each interval it reads the network's security metrics and the attacker's current attack action, and deploys one of four mechanisms (complete topology shuffle, IP shuffle, OS diversity or service diversity) or none; if 2 000 s pass without a deployment, one is forced .
A run ends when the attacker compromises more than 80 % of the hosts , compromises a target host in the targeted scenario, or can discover no new host.

On each host it tries stolen credentials first, then exploits the vulnerabilities in order of return on attack , an exploit's probability of success times its impact, divided by the time it takes , and brute force last.
When the list runs out, it scans for hosts again, and the new list holds every host it can reach, including those it has already tried.
Scanning for hosts, enumerating a host and scanning a host's neighbours each take 5 s, scanning its ports 25 s and brute force 20 s .
An exploit takes 15 s times one minus the vulnerability's attack complexity , which lies between 0.4 and 1 , so from 0 to 9 s.
Chapter 1 compares the baseline attacker, and the attacker models of recent MTD evaluations, with an APT attacker.
Section 1 describes MITRE ATT | CK, the knowledge base that records attacker behaviour as techniques.

In preparation, the attacker researches its target and builds its tools; in intrusion, it gains a foothold on a host in the target's network and runs its code there; in post-intrusion operations, it moves through the network undetected; in actions on objectives, it steals data or impedes the victim's systems.
MITRE ATT | CK is a knowledge base of attacker behaviour derived from real-world observations, developed by the MITRE Corporation in 2013 , and the common language for attacker behaviour .
ATT | CK organises behaviour into a hierarchy of tactics, techniques, sub-techniques and procedures .
A tactic is what an attacker does to achieve a goal, a technique is how it does it, and a procedure is one recorded instance of a technique .
The product of attack profiling, an attack profile, can be executed as an attacker in a simulation; Chapter 1 builds its APT attacker model on attack profiles.
This dissertation scores each attacker model on each property from its paper, by predicates taken from each definition in Table 1 (Appendix 1), with one of three marks.
At each deployment interval, the analytical model computes each attack path's success probability, cost and RoA, before and after the MTD deploys.
\paragraphKim et al. Kim et al. use a real testbed, a software-defined network on physical hardware, to evaluate an MTD that combines virtual IP shuffling, software diversity and redundancy .
None of the three has objective-specific behaviour, cost--benefit reasoning, learning or deployment-strategy awareness, and only Kim et al.'s has detection avoidance, in part.
The attacker models of Masud et al. and Kim et al., which this dissertation expected to be the most likely to have the properties, have none in full.

An attack action fails if its preconditions were missing (for example, an exploit of a vulnerability not yet scanned for), or if an MTD deployment disrupts it (Section 1).

Initial Access, Execution and Privilege Escalation each include a technique that exploits a vulnerability, so all three map to exploit, and Reconnaissance and Discovery each include a scanning technique, so Reconnaissance maps to scan host and Discovery to scan port.
They set how often the APT attacker model acts, and the longer a tactic runs, the more likely an MTD deployment disrupts it.
An exponential delay has one parameter, its mean, so each tactic needs one value, its mean duration x.

Initial Access, Privilege Escalation, Credential Access and Lateral Movement each act briefly on one host, as the exploit attack action does, so each takes the mean time of the exploit attack action, 4.5 s.
Reconnaissance and Discovery survey a network, as MTDSim's scans for hosts, ports and neighbours do together, so each takes the total time of the three scans, 35 s.
Persistence, Stealth and Command and Control keep a foothold, stay hidden and stay in contact throughout an attack , so we set them longest, at 45 s.
Collection, Exfiltration and Impact move or destroy data, which we judged to take a little longer than surveying a network, so we set them at 36 s.
Only the 45 s changes NCR much, most likely through Command and Control, one of the three tactics it times.
The slower the attacker finds new hosts, the fewer it reaches before the run ends, so Chapter 1's NCR rests most on this one value.
Third, an attacker seldom skips a lifecycle stage, as in the lifecycle models of Section 1, which run their stages in sequence.
Where the attack flows give a tactic no next tactic, a dead end, there is nothing to reweight, and the token retraces the edge it travelled.
It is not learning, property 7 of Table 1: it keeps vulnerabilities, not the patterns of MTD deployments, and it changes the odds of an exploit, not which technique comes next.
Each earlier success on a vulnerability, on any host, triples the attacker's odds of exploiting it again (the odds its attack complexity sets, Section 1).
Hosts that run the same service carry the same vulnerabilities, so we expect the memory to matter more when the diversity pool, the services each operating system can run, is small.
Section 1 tests this expectation, and finds that the memory raises the share of exploits that succeed, most with a small diversity pool, but leaves what the attacker achieves unchanged.
MTDSim detects no attacker, so the two metrics for detection avoidance measure it by proxy, through how often the attacker acts.
\paragraphAttack confidentiality. Attack rate is a mean, so it does not show bursts of attack actions, which an IDS flags.
MTDSim has no IDS, so one stands in with a single rule, the default port-scan rule of the Snort IDS, which flagged a source that connected to five different addresses within 60 s .
A deployment disrupts at most the attack action in progress, so the metric runs from 0, when no deployment disrupts one, to 1, when every deployment does.
\paragraphTime lost per MTD deployment. Time lost per MTD deployment, the metric for adaptivity, is how much an MTD deployment delays the attacker's next compromise of a host.
A deployment at 6 000 s, with the next compromise at 6 900 s under MTD and at 6 400 s with no MTD, costs the attacker 500 s.
